profile.bio:
I work on the engineering around the model: retrieval, evaluation, governed data access, latency, and deployment. At Cogent People I build agentic AI and AWS data systems for InsightAI, an enterprise healthcare analytics platform that lets people query complex business data in natural language.

Before that I spent nine months at Boundary Remote Subsurface Solutions on a production geospatial AI framework, fusing seismic, well-log, gravity, magnetic, and hyperspectral data. Different domain, same lesson: the quality of the data, the retrieval, and the evaluation loop usually matters more than the choice of model.

Rutgers, Magna Cum Laude, double major in Computer Science and Data Science.

projects.title: Decoding the Fed
projects.subtitle: Does FOMC language actually predict Treasury yields?
projects.problem: Central-bank tone is widely assumed to move rates, and NLP-on-FOMC papers are everywhere. Almost none of them report what the sentiment features are worth against a plain macro baseline, which makes the claimed gains impossible to judge.
projects.approach: Built an NLP and ML pipeline over 30 years of FOMC statements — FinBERT sentiment and TF-IDF keyword features joined to macro data — then ran every model against a deliberate 6-feature macro-only baseline across 9 targets (2Y, 10Y, 2s10s spread × 1-, 3-, 5-day horizons) under walk-forward validation. 54 model × target cells, with per-fold RMSE variance retained rather than averaged away.
projects.outcome: The best configuration (Random Forest, 2Y 1-day) reached 8.7 bps RMSE against an 11.0 bps macro baseline — a 21% improvement. But across the other eight targets the gains ranged from 0.8% to 10.6%, and fold-to-fold standard deviation (±4.3 bps) ran roughly double the model differences. The honest reading is that FOMC sentiment adds little over macro features once you validate properly. Reporting that was the point.

metrics.label: bps RMSE — best model vs macro baseline, 2Y 1-day

projects.title: RU-PATH
projects.subtitle: RAG assistant for Rutgers parking and transit
projects.problem: Rutgers parking and transit rules are scattered across PDFs, department pages, and route tables. Students routinely get it wrong, and the authoritative answer depends on lot, permit type, time of day, and campus.
projects.approach: Built a retrieval-augmented assistant over the scattered source documents — FAISS vector search feeding a DeepSeek-backed generation step through LangChain, served by FastAPI. Query handling was structured by intent category rather than treated as one flat retrieval problem.
projects.outcome: Handles 350+ distinct query types at roughly 89% response accuracy, with 99% uptime in production use. The accuracy gains came from retrieval and intent routing, not from the generation model.

projects.title: EvacAI
projects.subtitle: Disaster preparedness platform · IBM Z × UNSA Hackathon
projects.contribution: REPLACE ME — one sentence naming exactly what you built. Which services, which parts of the backend, what you owned versus what teammates owned.
projects.problem: During floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and earthquakes, the information people need is split across weather services, alert feeds, and shelter directories — at exactly the moment they have least capacity to assemble it.
projects.approach: A FastAPI backend that joins geocoding, live weather, active disaster alerts, and shelter resources into a single location query, with ML-based risk scoring and IBM watsonx/Granite generating an evacuation plan from the assembled context.
projects.outcome: Working platform with global location support, deployed as a web app with an accompanying iOS client.
